description: We are interested in creating a friendly way to learn about space!
summary: LEFTOVERS is a friendly web game that aims to teach a younger audience about the 15 NASA spacecraft left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space by letting each one tell its own story. The game starts with a cyber attack erasing Mission Control’s records of these leftover spacecrafts. The player is an astronaut who is motivated by this and sent to find these leftover spacecrafts and rebuild their records. Players fly to the Moon, Mars, and out across the solar system, and can check what the time on Earth is after each mission's trip. Every leftover waits at a simulated version of its real landing site. When a player is launched into space they select a destination and when they reach their destination there are glowing dots that represent each leftover. The player is prompted to click a dot and when it does the leftover comes to life and walks the player through its launch, landing, the science its crew did, and ends its story with where it sits today as a 3D model that you can interact with. All the information presented on LEFTOVERS is from NASA.
details:
What does LEFTOVERS do?
LEFTOVERS is a web game where the player is an astronaut rebuilding Mission Control’s records after a cyber attack erased them. The player lifts off from a launch pad on Earth and picks a destination once in space: the Moon, Mars or the whole solar system. During each trip, a Time on Earth clock jumps ahead by the real amount of time that the mission took to get to the players location (ex: four days to the Moon or eleven months to Mars). When the player completes their mission it shows the total amount of time they had been away for. When the player arrives, glowing dots show where each leftover is, placed at its real landing coordinates on a NASA globe. On the solar system map, the player can also tap the Sun or any planet to see a NASA picture and a fun fact about it.

When the player taps a dot and presses MY EYES, the leftover tells its own story in four chapters: LAUNCH, ARRIVAL, MY WORK and WHERE I WAS LEFT. Each chapter uses real NASA photos and videos, like the actual film from Apollo 11’s landing. The last chapter shows the leftover where it is today as a NASA 3D model that the player can drag around. The model has glowing dots on its parts, and each one explains what that part did, like the laser mirror on Apollo 11 that scientists still use to measure how far away the Moon is. The player has to explore every dot to finish the story, and then the record is restored. There is a button called Destinations in the top right corner that the player can press to go to the Moon, Mars, or Solar System at any time. Once all 15 leftovers are found, the player returns home and sees how much time passed on Earth during their whole mission.

How does it work?
LEFTOVERS is a web app built with React, Vite, JavaScript, and CSS. We also used three.js to show the globes, the trips and the 3D scenes using NASA’s 3D models and planet maps. The dots use each leftover’s real landing coordinates, and the clock uses each mission’s real launch and arrival dates. The trips also show what the ship would actually pass, like flying through the asteroid belt to reach Dawn, or passing Jupiter and Saturn on the way to Pioneer 11. The game saves progress in the browser, so there is no account or download, and it works on phones, tablets and computers.

What makes LEFTOVERS distinctive?
A lot of projects put spacecraft on a map or let them talk. LEFTOVERS is different because it turns learning about them into a full mission:

  • You actually travel to each leftover. The Time on Earth clock shows how long these missions really took, so by the end the player understands it took decades of work to put them there.
  • Each leftover has a personality. Sojourner says it is small but mighty and Pioneer 10 and 11 call each other sisters and tell the player to go find the other one.
  • The science is shown. Each story shows how the spacecraft did its job with real NASA footage, then lets the player explore the actual parts that made the discoveries.
  • Every fact is checked. Every statement was checked against a NASA page, and every photo, video and model shows where it came from right on the screen.

What are the benefits and the impact?
Most kids only hear about the missions happening now and if they want to learn about older ones they would need to read long technical pages with many unfamiliar words. LEFTOVERS makes that learning fun and easy. By the end, players know what each leftover is, why it was sent, how it worked and what it discovered. They also learn that some of them are still helping science today, like Eagle’s laser mirror and Kepler’s data. Since LEFTOVERS is free and needs no login, teachers can use it in class and kids can play it at home on any device.

What did our team consider?
We made LEFTOVERS for younger audience so the text boxes are short and harder words like dwarf planet, pulsar and gamma-ray spectrometer are explained simply. Tips show up whenever a screen might be confusing. Everything works with touch, mouse or keyboard. Images have descriptions and videos have captions, and there are settings for brightness, sound and music. There is also a warning before scenes with flashing lights. Accuracy was our biggest priority, so anything a NASA page did not support was changed or removed, and anything made with SI is labeled “SI Generated Content”.

What tools did we use?
React, Vite, JavaScript, CSS, three.js, @react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei and the Web Audio API, which makes the music and sound effects in code. The website’s code was written with the help of SI (Claude Code).
